![Analysis of the changes in answers after two rounds of self-correction. *No Change*: The answer remains unchanged; *Correct $\Rightarrow$ Incorrect*: A correct answer is changed to an incorrect one; *Incorrect $\Rightarrow$ Correct*: An incorrect answer is revised to a correct one; *Incorrect $\Rightarrow$ Incorrect*: An incorrect answer is altered but remains incorrect. Figure 1 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](cover.jpg){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="cover-full.jpg"}

In *Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet* [[1]](#ref-1) ([ICLR 2024](https://iclr.cc/Conferences/2024)), [Jie Huang](https://jeffhj.github.io/), [Xinyun Chen](https://xinyun-chen.github.io/), [Swaroop Mishra](https://swarooprm.github.io/), [Huaixiu Steven Zheng](https://stevenzheng.github.io/), [Adams Wei Yu](https://www.adamsyu.com/), Xinying Song, and [Denny Zhou](https://dennyzhou.github.io/) (Google DeepMind + UIUC) argue that *intrinsic self-correction* — where a model revises its own reasoning answer with no external signal about correctness — does not improve and often degrades performance on reasoning benchmarks.

> Large Language Models (LLMs) have emerged as a groundbreaking technology with their unparalleled text generation capabilities across various applications. Nevertheless, concerns persist regarding the accuracy and appropriateness of their generated content. A contemporary methodology, self-correction, has been proposed as a remedy to these issues. Building upon this premise, this paper critically examines the role and efficacy of self-correction within LLMs, shedding light on its true potential and limitations. Central to our investigation is the notion of *intrinsic self-correction, whereby an LLM attempts to correct its initial responses based solely on its inherent capabilities, without the crutch of external feedback*. In the context of reasoning, our research indicates that *LLMs struggle to self-correct their responses without external feedback, and at times, their performance even degrades after self-correction*. Drawing from these insights, we offer suggestions for future research and practical applications in this field.

## Methods

The paper isolates *intrinsic* self-correction by stripping out the external verifier that prior self-correction work relied on. In the **oracle setting** (used by RCI [[2]](#ref-2) and Reflexion [[3]](#ref-3) in their reported evaluations), the loop has access to the gold-label answer:

1. Model generates an answer.
2. Compare it to the ground truth (the oracle).
3. If correct, stop. If wrong, prompt the model for a critique, generate a revision, return to step 2.

The oracle is doing two jobs at once: it's a stopping condition (don't keep revising correct answers) and a trigger for revision (only revise when wrong). In the **intrinsic setting**, both jobs go away. The same model produces the initial answer, then is prompted to review and revise it without any external check, and has to decide on its own whether the answer needs further work. The evaluation runs on three reasoning datasets — GSM8K [[10]](#ref-10) (grade-school math), CommonSenseQA [[11]](#ref-11) (multiple-choice commonsense), and HotpotQA [[12]](#ref-12) (multi-hop QA) — across GPT-3.5-Turbo (`gpt-3.5-turbo-0613`), GPT-4, GPT-4-Turbo (`gpt-4-1106-preview`), and `Llama-2-70b-chat` [[4]](#ref-4). Each round of self-correction costs two additional model calls (review, then revision), so two rounds bring the total per question to five.

The paper then re-examines two related claims from prior work:

- **Section 4** revisits multi-agent debate [[5]](#ref-5), where several LLM agents propose answers and critique each other across rounds until they converge on a consensus. The paper reproduces Du et al. [[5]](#ref-5)'s setup on GSM8K and compares it against self-consistency [[6]](#ref-6) [[6]](#ref-6) — generating multiple independent samples and majority-voting — at the *same total response budget*.
- **Section 5** revisits Self-Refine [[7]](#ref-7) [[7]](#ref-7) <!-- crosslink-todo: /posts/20260503-self-refine/ -->, where the same LLM generates an output, critiques it, and refines based on its own critique over multiple iterations. The paper attributes Self-Refine's reported gains on constrained generation to a sub-optimal initial prompt that the refinement loop is largely just patching.

![Two GSM8K examples with GPT-3.5: a successful correction on the left, a failed one on the right where the model revises a correct answer into an incorrect one. The failure mode dominates the data. Figure 2 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](figure2.webp){fig-align="center" data-lightbox-src="figure2-full.png"}

## Results

- **Intrinsic self-correction degrades accuracy across every model tested.** With oracle labels (Table 2 of the paper), self-correction improves modestly — GPT-3.5 on GSM8K rises from 75.9 to 84.3, GPT-4 on HotpotQA from 49.0 to 59.0. Without oracle labels, the same prompts and models *lose* accuracy. After two rounds of intrinsic self-correction, GPT-3.5 on GSM8K drops from 75.9 to 74.7. On CommonSenseQA the drop is sharper, 75.8 to 41.8. GPT-4 holds up better but still loses 6.5 points on GSM8K (95.5 → 89.0). Llama-2-70b-chat collapses, halving from 62.0 to 36.5 on GSM8K. The cover image's Figure 1 decomposition shows why: correct → incorrect transitions outnumber incorrect → correct ones, so the loop is on average destructive.

![*Table 2* (top): Results of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on reasoning benchmarks with oracle labels. *Table 3* (bottom): Results of GPT-3.5 and GPT-4 on reasoning benchmarks with intrinsic self-correction. Tables 2 and 3 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](table2-3.png){fig-align="center"}

- **Multi-agent debate underperforms self-consistency at matched budget.** With three agents over two rounds of debate, the system uses nine total responses and reaches 83.0 on GSM8K. Self-consistency with nine responses reaches 88.2 with the same model. At every matched budget, simple majority voting beats the debate protocol. The paper concludes that what looks like critique is in practice a noisier form of consensus.

![*Table 7*: Results of multi-agent debate and self-consistency. Table 7 from the paper [[1]](#ref-1).](table7.png){fig-align="center"}

## My Notes

- **The RL follow-up.** Two follow-ups from this same group at Google DeepMind reframe the negative result rather than overturn it. [SCoRe](/posts/20260512-score/) [[8]](#ref-8) trains Gemini 1.0 Pro and 1.5 Flash via multi-turn RL to actually self-correct on MATH, gaining 15.6 points on top of the base model — explicitly citing this paper as the problem statement. The o1-style training paradigm builds correction into the chain-of-thought RL signal itself. The conclusion of *Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet* is essentially that prompting alone cannot induce self-correction in models that were not trained for it; the field has since shown that the right RL objective can.
- **The oracle-label confound is the methodological core.** The paper's most reusable contribution is naming the evaluation issue: RCI [[2]](#ref-2) [[2]](#ref-2) and Reflexion [[3]](#ref-3) [[3]](#ref-3) <!-- crosslink-todo: /posts/20260503-reflexion/ --> let the loop terminate based on whether the answer was correct, which leaks ground truth into the evaluation. Once you remove that signal, the loop runs without a stop condition and tends to drift. This generalizes: any test-time loop that uses the gold answer to decide when to halt is implicitly conditioning on it. The same issue surfaces in [process reward model evaluation](/posts/20260512-lets-verify-step-by-step/), where a strong external verifier carries most of the signal that gets attributed to the generator.
- **Production loops have implicit signals.** Real systems usually carry external signals that the paper's "no oracle" definition excludes: format checks, runnable code, type errors, schema violations, factual lookups against retrieval. Reflexion [[3]](#ref-3) [[3]](#ref-3) <!-- crosslink-todo: /posts/20260503-reflexion/ -->, for instance, uses an environment reward (test pass/fail, task success). The paper's negative result is for the strict version where the model has nothing to go on but its own prior; that is the version closest to "talking to yourself," which is also the version least likely to converge.
- **Multi-agent debate as ensembling.** Section 4's finding that multi-agent debate underperforms self-consistency at matched response budget [[5]](#ref-5)[[6]](#ref-6) has been replicated repeatedly since, across the multi-agent literature, including [the MAST taxonomy of multi-agent failure modes](/posts/20250802-mast-multi-agent-failures/) [[9]](#ref-9). Stripped of training, much of what looks like agent collaboration reduces to weighted voting on independent samples. What matters is the sampling budget, not the protocol.
